lines.text: Why does your phone die at thirty percent when it's cold?
Apple says a low charge, the cold or an old battery raises its impedance. Think of it as inner resistance.
Then the voltage sags the moment the phone asks for power, and the chips need a minimum voltage to keep running.
So the phone shuts itself down on purpose, to protect its parts, even when there's charge left.
It's only temporary. Once the battery warms back up, its performance returns to normal.
Apple says iPhones work best between zero and thirty-five degrees Celsius. Heat can harm a battery for good.
Cold pauses it. Keep it warm.

post.title: Why does your phone die at 30% in the cold?
post.caption:
Why does your phone die at 30% when it's cold? 🥶🔋 The percent is not the problem: the cold is.

Apple says a low charge, a higher chemical age or cold temperatures make a lithium-ion battery's impedance (inner resistance) rise. With high impedance the battery's voltage drops further when the phone pulls power, and the electronics need a minimum voltage to work, so the phone can shut down on purpose to protect them, even with charge left. The cold effect is temporary: once the battery warms back up to its normal range, performance returns. Apple says iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch work best at 0° to 35° C (32° to 95° F), and heat above 35° C can permanently damage battery capacity.

Send this to a friend who lives somewhere cold.
